claim: MRP for pre-election polling formally decomposes the estimation problem into three components: the conditional vote-choice distribution p(V|X,T=1), the conditional turnout distribution p(T=1|X), and the poststratification frame f(X) giving the population count of each demographic/political type X, then aggregates vote share as a weighted sum over all types rather than over sampled observations.
stance_target: formal statistical structure of MRP applied to elections
quoted_support: The crucial distinction between this approach, and the weighting approach followed by most polling, is seen by comparing Equations 1 and 2. In the weighting approach, the sum is over the sampled observations; in the modelling approach, the sum is over the set of voter types.

claim: MRP as applied to pre-election polling builds directly on Gelman & Little (1997) and Park, Gelman & Bafumi (2004), extending small-area public-opinion estimation methods (previously applied to US states, US congressional districts, German electoral districts, Swiss cantons, UK constituencies) to distinguish voters from non-voters within the estimation.
stance_target: theoretical lineage and prior applications of MRP
quoted_support: In this study, we describe our approach to applying the logic of multilevel regression and post-stratiﬁcation (MRP; Gelman and Little, 1997; Park et al., 2004) to pre-election polling.

claim: Across three applications published in advance of the events (2016 EU referendum, 2016 US presidential election, 2017 UK general election), the national vote-share margin errors were 2.6 percentage points, 1.7 percentage points, and 0.9 percentage points respectively.
stance_target: MRP can deliver low national-margin forecast error across diverse election types
scope_conditions: UK 2016 referendum, US 2016 presidential, UK 2017 general election
quoted_support: The magnitude of the errors on the national vote share margin between the top two alternatives were all reasonable (2.6% EU 2016, 1.7% US 2016, 0.9% UK 2017), but we acknowledge that it is possible to get lucky on a single outcome quantity in three elections.

claim: In the 2016 EU referendum application, the model's local-authority-level estimates correlated with actual results at r=0.92, despite the complete lack of any directly comparable past referendum result to use as a poststratification/turnout anchor.
stance_target: MRP can generalise to novel electoral questions lacking direct historical precedent at the sub-national level
scope_conditions: UK, 2016 EU referendum, local authority level
quoted_support: In the EU referendum, we generated local authority level estimates that correlated with the results at r=0.92, despite the lack of any directly comparable past electoral results.

claim: In the 2016 US presidential election, the MRP model's point estimate favored a narrow Clinton popular-vote win, but the model correctly identified that Trump's Electoral College advantage made a Trump victory the most likely scenario even while losing the national popular vote — despite the Electoral College advantage having favored Obama in 2012.
stance_target: MRP's sub-national estimates can surface structural electoral-system dynamics that simple national polling averages miss
quoted_support: the model correctly identiﬁed Trump's electoral college advantage—even though the electoral college advantage in 2012 was in Obama's favour—and therefore that Trump's most likely victory scenarios involved losing the national popular vote.

claim: The UK 2017 general election MRP model was the only pre-election seat forecast that correctly indicated the Conservatives would fail to secure a parliamentary majority.
stance_target: MRP outperformed all alternative pre-election forecasting approaches in the highest-stakes binary outcome of the 2017 UK election
quoted_support: Indeed, they were the only pre-election seat forecast that correctly indicated that the Conservatives would fail to secure a majority.

claim: The authors identify a general problem of attenuation bias in MRP: a tendency to underpredict a party's/option's strength where it is strong and overpredict where it is weak, only partially mitigated via cross-level interactions between individual-level and constituency/district-level past vote, with mixed success across the three applications.
stance_target: MRP produces uniformly well-calibrated sub-national estimates without systematic bias
scope_conditions: MRP applied to UK 2016/2017 and US 2016 elections
quoted_support: there is a general problem of attenuation bias: the tendency to underpredict voting alternatives where they are strong and overpredict them where they are weak. We were able to partially mitigate this through the use of cross-level interactions of individual and constituency/district vote, with varying success across applications.

claim: The authors document undercoverage of interval estimates at the constituency/district level across all three applications, because non-sampling error is difficult to fold into properly calibrated uncertainty intervals even when point-estimate error magnitudes are small.
stance_target: MRP's reported confidence intervals are well-calibrated at fine geographic granularity
scope_conditions: MRP applied to UK 2016/2017 and US 2016 elections
quoted_support: we see undercoverage of the constituency/district level results in all our applications. The diﬃculty of incorporating uncertainty due to non-sampling errors into the model estimation makes it diﬃcult to generate properly calibrated interval estimates, even when error magnitudes are not large.

claim: A major acknowledged limitation of the Lauderdale et al. MRP strategy is that it does not attempt to model shifts in turnout patterns at either the individual or aggregate level, treating the voting population's composition as static, on the grounds that self-reported likelihood-to-vote is unreliable without richer validated panel/turnout data.
stance_target: MRP as implemented in this canonical framework fully captures turnout dynamics that shift between elections
scope_conditions: MRP framework as implemented by Lauderdale, Bailey, Blumenau, Rivers 2017
quoted_support: a major limitation of our strategy is that we do not attempt to model shifs in turnout patterns at either the individual or aggregate level. While this avoids large errors in the modelled voting population, and we believe there are good reasons to be skeptical of naive use of self-reported likelihood to turnout, given suitably rich panel data on likelihood to vote, combined with validated turnout data, it should be possible to improve on this strategy.

claim: Wang et al. (2014) applied MRP to the 2012 US presidential election using an unusually large but unrepresentative sample (750,000 responses from an Xbox poll, 93% male, 65% aged 18-29) averaging 15,000 observations per state — a sample size so large it undercuts MRP's core value proposition of borrowing statistical strength across sparse sub-national units.
stance_target: the strength of MRP's evidentiary contribution depends on genuinely sparse per-unit sample sizes, not just large aggregate samples
scope_conditions: US, 2012 presidential election, Xbox poll sample
quoted_support: those authors used an unusually large sample—750,000 responses—from an unusually unrepresentative data source—an XBox poll with a 93% male and 65% 18-29 years old sample... it is not the most convincing illustration of the power of model-based methods for generating small area estimates, as that study used an average of 15,000 observations per state.

claim: Comparing the two sub-national applications, the UK 2017 general election model (632 constituencies) outperformed the US 2016 presidential model (51 states) despite far less raw survey data per US state, plausibly because 632 constituencies support more covariates at the second (geographic) level of the multilevel regression and provide more opportunity for prediction errors to counterbalance, whereas widely varying US state electoral-vote counts make the aggregate outcome highly sensitive to a handful of errant state-level estimates.
stance_target: the number and granularity of sub-national electoral units affects MRP's aggregate reliability independent of per-unit data volume
scope_conditions: comparison of UK 632-constituency and US 51-state MRP applications, 2016-2017
quoted_support: it may be that constructing good estimates for 51 states is actually more diﬃcult than for 632 constituencies, because the latter support more covariates at the second level of the multilevel regression and provide greater opportunity for errors to counter-balance. The widely varying state electoral votes make close US elections extremely sensitive to a few errant state results.

claim: Constituency polling is essentially absent in most UK election cycles, meaning national aggregation-based poll averaging (effective in the multi-state-polled US context) does not translate to reliable sub-national UK estimates: only in the 2015 cycle were a non-trivial number of constituency polls conducted, and even then covering only about 20% of constituencies over the full year preceding the election.
stance_target: UK electoral geography structurally requires model-based (rather than poll-aggregation) approaches for constituency-level estimation
scope_conditions: UK general elections, constituency polling frequency
quoted_support: In only one election cycle (2015) have a non-trivial number of constituency polls been conducted, and even then only about 20% of constituencies over the entire year preceding the election.

claim: In the 2017 UK general election, the relationship between educational qualifications and vote-switching was substantial: the Conservatives retained about 90% of their 2015 voters with lower qualification levels but only 80% of those with higher qualification levels, and gained larger shares of Liberal Democrat and Labour voters with low qualifications than those with high qualifications.
stance_target: education is a strong, differentially predictive covariate for vote-switching patterns usable in MRP poststratification
quoted_support: In the 2017 general election, the Conservatives retained about 90% of their 2015 voters with lower levels of qualiﬁcations, but only 80% of those with higher levels of qualiﬁcations. They also gained larger shares of the Liberal Democrat and Labour voters with low levels of qualiﬁcations than those with high.

claim: In the 2016 EU referendum, support for Leave among those with no qualifications was about 20 percentage points higher than among those with a university degree or higher (Level 4+), and the qualification-based gap for 2015 Labour, Liberal Democrat, and SNP/Plaid Cymru supporters was even larger, reaching 30-40 percentage points.
stance_target: education level is a strongly predictive demographic covariate for the Leave/Remain vote in the UK
quoted_support: with no qualiﬁcations (less than GCSEs or equiv) support for Leave was about 20 points higher than among those with Level 4+ (BA or higher qualiﬁcations). For Labour, Liberal Democrat and SNP/PC 2015 supporters, these diﬀerences were even larger, reaching 30-40 points.
